title: Regression and prediction
subtitle: Fit a line, read its slope, predict, and see how one outlier can betray it.

idea.title: Predicting a number
idea.body: Regression predicts a continuous target y from features x. Simple linear regression: ŷ = a + bx. The slope b is “change in y per unit x”; the intercept a is y at x = 0. Classification, by contrast, predicts a category.

fit.title: Least squares
fit.body: Choose a, b minimising the sum of squared residuals. For the sample data slope = 0.9, intercept = 1.3, R² = 0.81.
fit.steps: Slope b = Sxy / Sxx = 9 / 10. Intercept a = ȳ − b x̄ = 4 − 0.9·3.

outl.title: Outliers can steer the line
outl.body: Replace the last point (5, 6) with (5, 30): slope jumps to 5.7 and R² falls to 0.5732. Squaring makes big errors dominate; robust methods or removing a verified error is the remedy.

metrics.title: Measuring error
metrics.body: MAE = mean |error|; MSE = mean error²; RMSE = √MSE (same units as y); R² = 1 − SSres/SStot. RMSE punishes large errors more than MAE. Always compare to a baseline: predicting the mean has R² = 0.
metrics.steps: Errors: 1, −2, 3. MSE = (1 + 4 + 9)/3 = 4.67, so RMSE = 2.16 while MAE = 2.

multi.title: Many features and overfitting
multi.body: ŷ = b₀ + b₁x₁ + … + b_k x_k. Adding features always lowers training error, but a model that memorises noise (overfits) does worse on new data. Regularisation (ridge/lasso) adds a penalty on large coefficients; validation (next chapter) detects the problem.

logi.title: From regression to classification
logi.body: To predict a yes/no outcome, pass the linear score through the sigmoid σ(s) = 1/(1 + e⁻ˢ) to get a probability in (0, 1), then threshold at 0.5. It is fitted by gradient descent, exactly as in chapter 2.
